description: For this challenge, we are exploring how satellite radar data can help us understand changes happening on Earth's surface. The goal is to build a useful, interactive tool that makes these observations easier to explore, even for people without a background in remote sensing.
summary:
LANDSHIFT is an interactive exploration tool that uses NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band GCOV radar observations to visualize differences in surface backscatter over time.

The prototype focuses on Merja Zerga lagoon, Morocco, comparing two observations acquired on August 26 and September 7, 2026, twelve days apart. Users can explore the observations and visualize where smoothed radar backscatter became brighter or darker.

The comparison identifies 108,673 of the 2,400,564 pixels treated as valid by the analysis (4.53%) with smoothed backscatter differences exceeding an operational ±3 dB threshold. These are radar differences, not confirmation of a specific environmental event or its cause.

LANDSHIFT demonstrates how interactive visualization can make satellite radar comparisons more accessible and support further investigation. The current version is a single-location case study, with broader geographic applications as a future direction.
details:
LANDSHIFT is an interactive web application that explores changes in Earth's surface radar backscatter using NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band GCOV observations.

The prototype focuses on Merja Zerga lagoon in Morocco. It processes two NISAR observations acquired on August 26 and September 7, 2026, twelve days apart. Users can explore the radar observations, compare them through an interactive before-and-after slider, and switch between radar backscatter and radar change visualizations.

The processing workflow uses Python and scientific libraries including NumPy, SciPy, h5py, and pyproj to work with the satellite data, perform geospatial processing, smooth radar measurements, and calculate pixel-level differences. The application presents these results through an interactive interface designed to make complex satellite observations easier to explore and understand.

The comparison identifies pixels whose smoothed backscatter differences exceed an operational ±3 dB threshold. In this study area, 108,673 out of 2,400,564 valid pixels (4.53%) exceed that threshold. Brighter and darker radar responses are visualized separately to help users investigate spatial patterns.

LANDSHIFT's main benefit is making satellite radar comparisons more accessible through an intuitive visual experience. Rather than presenting users with raw scientific datasets, it provides an interactive way to examine observations and identify areas that may warrant further investigation.

Scientific limitations were an important consideration. A difference in radar backscatter does not independently establish what physical change occurred or its cause. The results are not presented as confirmed flooding, drought, water-area change, or environmental damage. The current prototype is a single-location case study, not a global monitoring system.

The project combines satellite Earth observation, scientific data processing, geospatial visualization, and interactive web design. Python libraries used include NumPy, SciPy, h5py, and pyproj. The application is deployed on Netlify.

AI tools, including Claude and ChatGPT, assisted with development, code, and project design. Their contributions were reviewed and tested by the project creator and are disclosed on the application's About page.

LANDSHIFT aims to demonstrate how accessible, interactive tools can help people explore satellite observations and better understand how our planet's surface changes.
